lessons.title: Understanding GPAI models
lessons.subtitle: When a model falls under Chapter V, and which duties land on its provider

sections.title: What is a GPAI model, and who is its provider?
sections.content:
A **general-purpose AI model** (GPAI model) performs many different tasks and can be built into many downstream systems, as GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama or Mistral do (recitals 97 to 99, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689). Its **provider** develops it, or has it developed, and places it on the market under its own name. Articles 53 to 55 address that provider.

When a machinery company wires GPT-4 into its support chatbot through the OpenAI API, OpenAI stays the model provider. The company may be the **downstream provider** of the chatbot (Article 3, point 68): Article 53 does not reach it, and its Article 50 duty depends on its role and how it supplies the chatbot.

Most SMEs are **deployers** when they only use a system, or downstream providers when they build a model in, sometimes both.

sections.title: The four provider duties in Article 53
sections.content:
Article 53(1) gives every GPAI provider four duties, whether or not the model presents systemic risk:

- **Technical documentation** (point (a)) under Annex XI, including training and evaluation processes, kept current and available to the AI Office and national authorities on request.
- **Information for downstream providers** (point (b)) under Annex XII, so they understand the model's capabilities and limits and can meet their own duties.
- **Copyright policy** (point (c)), including reservations of rights under Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790.
- **Training-content summary** (point (d)), sufficiently detailed and published using the AI Office template.

**Free and open-source exception** (Article 53(2)): qualifying models under a free and open-source licence can be exempt from points (a) and (b), never with systemic risk. Points (c) and (d) always apply.

**Third-country providers** appoint an **authorised representative in the Union** before placing a GPAI model on the Union market (Article 54(1)), subject to the exception in Article 54(6).

sections.title: How GPAI duties affect downstream SMEs
sections.content:
Article 53 may not reach you, but you depend on it: without the model documentation and the training-content summary from the model provider, a downstream provider can neither assess system risk nor meet the duties of its own system.

**Vendor-review evidence:**

- Is the model provider a **Code of Practice signatory**, and which chapters did it sign (see lesson 2)? The official list sits on `digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu`.
- Is the **downstream documentation** under Annex XII available?
- Has the provider published a **training-content summary** using the AI Office template?
- Where required, is an **authorised representative in the Union** named under Article 54(1)?

A signature evidences stated commitments, not proof of compliance or a general quality rating. Use it as a first filter before you read the documentation and the contract. (Source: AI Office, General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, 10 July 2025; Article 53(4), Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.)

quiz.questionText: A machinery company builds GPT-4 into its support chatbot through the OpenAI API. Is it thereby a GPAI provider under Article 53?

answerOptions.text: Yes, because it uses the model commercially
No. OpenAI stays the provider; the company may be a downstream provider
Yes, as soon as it uses the model for customer support
No. It is only a deployer with no duties

quiz.explanation: The GPAI provider develops the model and places it on the market under its own name, here OpenAI. The machinery company may be a downstream provider of the chatbot (Article 3, point 68).

quiz.questionText: Which duties may be lifted for a qualifying open-source GPAI model without systemic risk?

answerOptions.text: Every duty in Article 53(1)
Only the copyright policy, point (c)
Technical documentation and downstream information, points (a) and (b)
The training-content summary, point (d)

quiz.explanation: Article 53(2) exempts qualifying open-source models without systemic risk from points (a) and (b). The copyright policy and training-content summary, points (c) and (d), always apply.

quiz.questionText: What must a US-based provider generally do before placing its GPAI model on the Union market?

answerOptions.text: Host the model on a server in the Union
Appoint an authorised representative in the Union under Article 54(1)
Obtain prior approval from a national supervisory authority
Release the model under an open-source licence

quiz.explanation: Article 54(1) requires an authorised representative in the Union beforehand, as contact point for the AI Office and authorities. Article 54(6) exempts qualifying open-source models without systemic risk.

lessons.title: Systemic risk and the GPAI Code of Practice
lessons.subtitle: What changes above 10^25 FLOPs, and why it reaches you anyway

sections.title: When does a GPAI model present systemic risk?
sections.content:
Above 10^25 floating-point operations of cumulative training compute, Article 51(2) presumes high-impact capabilities. Two routes lead to a **GPAI model with systemic risk** (Article 51(1)):

- **Point (a): high-impact capabilities**, evaluated with appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks.
- **Point (b): a Commission decision** based on the criteria in Annex XIII, taken ex officio or after a qualified alert from the scientific panel.

The Commission may amend the threshold by delegated act (Article 51(3)), and the provider may argue against classification. A model name settles nothing; check the Commission decision, the provider information and the model version. Using such a model does not make you its GPAI provider.

Which authority is responsible for an AI system built on a GPAI model depends on the provider, the system, the role, the sector and the specific rules in Article 88.

sections.title: Notification and the additional duties in Article 55
sections.content:
Where a model meets the threshold, or is expected to, the provider notifies the Commission **without delay and in any event within two weeks** (Article 52(1)). Under Article 52(2) it may argue that the model exceptionally presents no systemic risk; the Commission may reject that.

**Additional duties in Article 55(1)**, on top of Articles 53 and 54:

- state-of-the-art model evaluation, including adversarial testing
- assess and mitigate systemic risks at Union level
- report serious incidents to the AI Office and, where appropriate, national authorities
- adequate cybersecurity for the model and its physical infrastructure

The Chapter V GPAI duties have applied since **2 August 2025**. The Commission's power to fine GPAI model providers applies from **2 August 2026**.

sections.title: The GPAI Code of Practice
sections.content:
The AI Office published the **General-Purpose AI Code of Practice** on **10 July 2025** after a multi-stakeholder process, in three chapters: Transparency, Copyright, and Safety and Security.

The Code is **voluntary**. Until a harmonised standard is published, a provider may rely on it to demonstrate compliance with its obligations (Article 53(4)); no legal presumption of conformity follows. Signatory lists and signed chapters change, so check the current AI Office page.

quiz.questionText: Which value marks the presumption threshold for a GPAI model with systemic risk?

answerOptions.text: 10^23 floating-point operations of training compute
More than 10^25 floating-point operations of training compute (Article 51(2))
1 billion parameters
100 million users worldwide

quiz.explanation: Article 51(2) presumes high-impact capabilities above 10^25 floating-point operations of cumulative training compute. The Commission may amend the threshold by delegated act under Article 51(3).

quiz.questionText: Within what period must a GPAI provider notify the Commission that its model meets, or will meet, the systemic-risk threshold?

answerOptions.text: Within 72 hours
Within one month
Without delay and in any event within two weeks (Article 52(1))
In its next annual report

quiz.explanation: Article 52(1) requires notification without delay and in any event within two weeks. It must show that the condition in Article 51(1), point (a), is met.

quiz.questionText: When was the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice published?

answerOptions.text: 2 February 2025
10 July 2025
2 August 2025
2 August 2026

quiz.explanation: The AI Office published it on 10 July 2025. It can demonstrate compliance under Article 53(4) but creates no legal presumption of conformity.

lessons.title: Article 4 as an organisational duty
lessons.subtitle: Why the duty sits with management

sections.title: The wording and scope of Article 4
sections.content:
Article 4(1) of the AI Act requires **providers and deployers** to take measures to support the development of AI literacy among their staff and others acting on their behalf, considering knowledge, experience, training, use context and the people affected. **The addressee is the organisation.**

Under **Article 3, point 56**, AI literacy is the skills, knowledge and understanding needed to use AI systems in an informed way and to be aware of their opportunities, risks and possible harm.

Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since **27 July 2026**, makes clear that providers and deployers need **not guarantee a particular individual level of AI literacy**; the duty to take context-appropriate measures stands.

Article 4 has applied since **2 February 2025** and names no standard and no certification. Record your role- and risk-appropriate measures.

sections.title: How this differs from an introductory AI course
sections.content:
Stage 2 of this learning path, the Everyday AI Literacy course, teaches the individual the basics and can be one building block for Article 4. The duty itself sits with management: it works out who needs which knowledge and evidences the measures through policy, process, roles and records.

Training alone is not enough. What carries weight is a **documented learning policy** built on role, prior knowledge, risk and use context, with proportionate review and evidence. Article 4 prescribes no particular programme design and no refresher interval.

sections.title: Five implementation components
sections.content:
One way to implement Article 4:

1. **AI inventory and needs analysis:** which AI systems run here, in which risk context, and who works with them how deeply? The output is a list with role mapping.
2. **AI policy:** in writing, what staff may do, such as no confidential data in external LLMs, output checked before it reaches a customer, an escalation route for errors.
3. **Role-specific learning programme:** a common baseline, then depth for power users, managers and people with AI responsibilities where the needs analysis supports it.
4. **Evidence and review trail:** participants, content, dates, trainers, review timing, onboarding. In front of an authority, what counts is what you can show.
5. **Supplier information:** contracts with your HR, accounting or office software vendors settle which AI features are built in and which material comes with them.

quiz.questionText: Who is addressed by the duty in Article 4(1) of the AI Act?

answerOptions.text: Every employee individually
Providers and deployers of AI systems
Only the organisation's designated AI officer
Only providers of GPAI models

quiz.explanation: Article 4(1) addresses providers and deployers, meaning the organisation. As with occupational safety or Article 32 GDPR, the employer carries the duty.

quiz.questionText: Which measure alone does not show that Article 4 is met in the organisation's context?

answerOptions.text: One generic online course for everyone, without needs analysis or records
A role-specific learning programme supported by implementation records
A written AI policy combined with context-appropriate learning measures
A combined needs analysis, policy, and supplier-information review

quiz.explanation: A single generic course ignores the factors Article 4 names: knowledge, experience, training, use context and affected people. Article 4 asks for supportive organisational measures, not a guaranteed individual competence level.

quiz.questionText: Since when has Article 4 applied, and when do supervision and enforcement begin per the Commission FAQ?

answerOptions.text: Article 4 since 1 August 2024; enforcement from 2 February 2025
Article 4 since 2 February 2025; enforcement from early August 2026
Article 4 only from 2 August 2026, together with enforcement
Both begin on 2 August 2027

quiz.explanation: Article 4 has applied since 2 February 2025, as amended from 27 July 2026 by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. Per the Commission FAQ, supervision and enforcement begin in early August 2026. Article 99 sets no fixed fine per Article 4 shortcoming.

lessons.title: Transparency and machine-readable marking under Article 50
lessons.subtitle: Who marks the output and who discloses the use: provider and deployer, kept apart

sections.title: The four transparency duties in Article 50
sections.content:
Article 50 of the AI Act splits four transparency duties between provider and deployer:

- **Paragraph 1, AI-interaction notice (provider):** systems intended to interact directly with people are designed so the people concerned know they are interacting with AI, unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person.
- **Paragraph 2, machine-readable marking (provider, GPAI included):** systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text mark their outputs in a machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated, effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible. Assistive functions for standard editing and systems that do not substantially alter the input are exempt.
- **Paragraph 3, emotion recognition and biometric categorisation (deployer):** deployers inform the people exposed, except in law enforcement.
- **Paragraph 4, deepfakes and certain AI text (deployer):** deepfake images, audio and video are disclosed, with limited rules for evidently artistic, satirical or fictional works. AI text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must be disclosed too, unless it underwent human review or editorial control and someone holds editorial responsibility.

Article 50 applies **from 2 August 2026**.

sections.title: Who marks, who discloses
sections.content:
The split in Article 50 follows the technology:

- **Machine-readable marking happens as the content is generated.** Article 50(2) therefore puts it on the **provider** of the generating system or model.
- **Deepfake disclosure is decided at publication.** Article 50(4) therefore puts it on the **deployer**, such as the marketing agency that creates and posts the video.

Use an image-generation tool and publish the output, and you are the deployer for that use. Article 50(4) applies only to deepfakes and specified public-interest text; not every synthetic image is a deepfake. The provider's marking does not replace your disclosure.

An organisation that provides an AI system and also deploys it for its own outputs can owe duties in both roles. Record the role per system and per use.

sections.title: Operational implementation
sections.content:
What has to stand by 2 August 2026:

- **AI-interaction notice (paragraph 1):** at the latest at the first interaction, clear, distinguishable and accessible (Article 50(5)). The provider builds it in; the deployer checks that it still works in its own integration.
- **Machine-readable marking (paragraph 2):** the provider picks a suitable solution, such as C2PA; Article 50 does not mandate one technology. Deployers ask which marking the version produces and whether their publication workflow preserves it.
- **Deepfake disclosure (paragraph 4):** before publishing, the deployer checks whether the content is a deepfake and how to disclose it.
- **Transparency Code:** the voluntary Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content of **10 June 2026** supports Article 50(2), (4) and (5); it does not replace the case-by-case assessment.
- **Penalties:** infringements of Article 50 can draw up to EUR 15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover under Article 99(4), whichever is higher; for SMEs the lower amount applies (Article 99(6)).

quiz.questionText: An agency uses Midjourney to create and publish a hyperrealistic ad video of a real actor. Which Article 50 duties may apply?

answerOptions.text: Only the agency, for Article 50(2) and (4)
The provider marks (50(2)); the agency discloses a deepfake (50(4))
Only Midjourney has duties because the agency is an end customer
No one, as long as no natural person is depicted

quiz.explanation: Article 50(2) puts machine-readable marking on the provider of the generating system; Article 50(4) puts deepfake disclosure on the deployer. The two run in parallel.

quiz.questionText: Does Article 50(1) require another AI-interaction notice when a voice hotline opens with 'Welcome to the AI information service'?

answerOptions.text: Yes, always and without exception
No, the duty never applies to voice systems
No, where the AI interaction is obvious; the opening line indicates that
Only if the caller asks whether it is AI

quiz.explanation: Article 50(1) does not apply where the AI interaction is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person. An opening line naming the service as AI informs callers directly.

quiz.questionText: When does Article 50 apply, and what fine ceiling applies to infringements under Article 99(4)?

answerOptions.text: From 2 February 2025, with fines of up to EUR 5 million
From 2 August 2026; max. EUR 15 million or 3% of turnover
From 2 August 2025 together with the GPAI duties
From 2 August 2027 after a transition period

quiz.explanation: Article 113 makes Article 50 applicable from 2 August 2026. Infringements under Article 99(4) can draw up to EUR 15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher; for SMEs the lower amount applies (Article 99(6)).

props.title: Which transparency failure occurred?
props.scenario: Five everyday situations in which Article 50 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 may apply. Classify the transparency failure in each case.

modes.label: Missing AI disclosure
modes.desc: AI-generated content or an AI interaction is not disclosed where the law requires it.

modes.label: Not machine-readable
modes.desc: A human-readable notice exists, but the machine-readable marking under Article 50(2) is missing.

modes.label: Unnecessary disclosure
modes.desc: A disclosure is added where the identified duty does not apply.

modes.label: Wrong addressee
modes.desc: The duty is assigned to another role without checking who is provider or deployer.

cases.prompt: Your website's customer-service chatbot greets visitors with: Hello, I am Lisa from the service team.
cases.output: The bot presents itself as a human employee; no AI notice appears.
cases.why: Article 50(1) requires that people know they are interacting with AI, unless that is obvious.

cases.prompt: Your marketing agency publishes an AI-generated advertising video containing a realistic testimonial from a real person.
cases.output: No statement that the scene was artificially generated or manipulated.
cases.why: If the video is a deepfake, Article 50(4) requires the deployer to disclose that it was artificially generated or manipulated.

cases.prompt: Your company's tool generates AI text and records the origin only in a clearly visible PDF footnote.
cases.output: The text carries no machine-readable marking of its AI origin.
cases.why: Article 50(2) requires the provider to mark outputs in a machine-readable format; a human-readable footnote is not enough.

cases.prompt: Your internal tool summarises meeting notes only for the team.
cases.output: Every summary carries a large AI-generated notice, as if it were published.
cases.why: The Article 50(4) text duty covers publications on matters of public interest, not an internal summary. The provider's Article 50(2) marking is a separate question.

cases.prompt: You deploy a purchased chatbot and assume, without checking, that the AI notice is solely the manufacturer's job.
cases.output: No AI notice appears on the website; nobody checked the integration.
cases.why: Article 50(1) binds the provider. The deployer still checks that the supplied notice reaches users in its integration.
